article_title: China's Origin Data Goes Electronic: The 1 December 2026 Deadline for RCEP Importers
text: What changes on 1 December 2026?
answer: From that date, an importer who wants goods released before the electronic origin data is confirmed must apply for a duty guarantee rather than entering the missing origin data manually. Between 1 June and 30 November 2026, the manual route through the preferential trade agreement origin declaration system remains available, with the certificate uploaded electronically. From 1 December, the guarantee becomes the mechanism for advance release, and it is refunded once the data is confirmed as transmitted through the online certificate status query. Declarations filed on paper continue to require the paper certificate.

article_title: China's Origin Data Goes Electronic: The 1 December 2026 Deadline for RCEP Importers
text: How much does the duty guarantee actually cost?
answer: Less than most importers assume. On a $60,000 shipment carrying a 10% duty rate, the guarantee is $6,000 lodged for however long the data takes to confirm. At a 12% annual funding cost over 45 days, that is $88.77 — about 15 basis points of shipment value. The guarantee is returned once the data is verified, so the cost is the funding cost of the cash, not the duty itself. The number to worry about is the $6,000, which becomes real duty if the certificate never verifies.

article_title: China's Origin Data Goes Electronic: The 1 December 2026 Deadline for RCEP Importers
text: Does this apply to imports from other ASEAN countries?
answer: Announcement No. 74 of 2026 covers the China–Malaysia corridor specifically. It is the latest step in a sequence that began with paperless preferential origin declaration in 2021, and the mechanism is the one China has been building with free trade agreement partners individually. Importers in other ASEAN markets are not subject to this announcement today, and the operational end state it describes is the template those corridors are heading towards. Building the supplier-side verification habit now costs nothing and transfers directly.

article_title: China's Origin Data Goes Electronic: The 1 December 2026 Deadline for RCEP Importers
text: My supplier still issues paper certificates. Is that allowed?
answer: Yes. The announcement explicitly preserves paper declaration, and an importer choosing that route submits the paper origin certificate at the time of declaration. What paper does not do is exempt you from the data question. The electronic exchange concerns the data behind the certificate, not the medium you file in, and a paper certificate whose underlying record has not been transmitted runs into the same verification problem. The safe assumption is that the data requirement is independent of the filing format.

article_title: Section 301 Exclusions Expire November 9: The Duty Cliff, Dated and Priced
text: One date decides it: goods entered before 11:59 p.m. Eastern on 9 November 2026 clear under the exclusion; goods entered after it pay the full list rate, with no in-transit relief for cargo already at sea.

article_title: Section 301 Exclusions Expire November 9: The Duty Cliff, Dated and Priced
text: What exactly changes on 10 November 2026?
answer: Entries filed on or after that date lose the Section 301 product exclusion and pay the underlying list rate: 25% for goods on Lists 1, 2 and 3, and 7.5% for goods on List 4A, in addition to the most-favoured-nation duty already owed. There is no phase-in, no transition rate and nothing to apply for. The change is automatic, and it turns on the entry date rather than the date goods were ordered, shipped or unloaded. A container that sails in October and clears on 12 November pays the full rate.

article_title: Section 301 Exclusions Expire November 9: The Duty Cliff, Dated and Priced
text: My goods arrive before the deadline but clear after it. Does the exclusion still apply?
answer: No. Eligibility follows the date merchandise is entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, and the extension notice contains no in-transit savings clause. Goods on the water on 9 November receive no protection from having shipped while the exclusion was alive. If you have bonded stock of excluded goods, the withdrawal date is the entry date for this purpose, so inventory that qualifies today loses the exclusion on withdrawals made 10 November or later, even if it has been sitting in the warehouse for months.

article_title: Section 301 Exclusions Expire November 9: The Duty Cliff, Dated and Priced
text: Does my Section 301 exclusion protect me from the 2026 forced-labour tariffs?
answer: No, and this is the most common misreading of the two headings. The 9903.88.69 and 9903.88.70 exclusions apply only to the technology-transfer investigation that produced Lists 1 to 4A. The forced-labour action that took effect for entries on or after 24 July 2026 is a separate determination with its own exemption annexes, and it applies an additional duty to products of 54 economies including China regardless of exclusion status. Check that annex against your headings before assuming the exclusion clears the whole entry.

article_title: Section 301 Exclusions Expire November 9: The Duty Cliff, Dated and Priced
text: Can my broker fix an entry that missed the exclusion?
answer: Only while the correction window is open, and never by changing the entry date. A Post Summary Correction can be filed within 300 days of the entry date and up to 15 days before scheduled liquidation, provided the entry is paid and not under review. That is the mechanism for an entry filed before the cutoff where the exclusion was available and not claimed. Once an entry liquidates, the route is a protest within 180 days of liquidation. No correction retroactively makes a 15 November entry eligible for an exclusion that ended on 9 November.

text: Nine points, two dates: three points removed in April 2026 and six more on 1 January 2027. On a $40 unit that is $3.60, and the only question that matters is how much of it your supplier intends to price into your next order.

article_title: China Is Removing the Export Rebate That Funded Cheap Quotes
text: Does the export tax rebate change appear on my invoice?
answer: No, and that is why it is easy to miss. The rebate is a refund paid by the Chinese tax authority to the exporter, calculated on the export value. It reduces the supplier's net cost, so it influences the FOB price rather than appearing as a line item. When the rate falls, the supplier's net receipt on an unchanged invoice falls with it, and the supplier decides how much to recover through price. The buyer sees the consequence as a higher quotation, with no line that explains it. Asking the supplier to identify it explicitly is the only way to see the number.

article_title: China Is Removing the Export Rebate That Funded Cheap Quotes
text: Which products are affected?
answer: The announcement covers photovoltaic products and battery-related products. Photovoltaic goods lost their export VAT rebate from 1 April 2026. Battery-related products ran at a 9% rebate, moved to 6% on the same date, and lose the remaining six points on 1 January 2027. The announcement adjusts rebates on a range of products including these two groups, so buyers in adjacent categories should check their own product codes rather than assuming the change is confined to solar and batteries.

article_title: China Is Removing the Export Rebate That Funded Cheap Quotes
text: How much of the increase will my supplier pass on?
answer: That is a commercial decision, not a published one, and it is the question worth asking before you place an order rather than after. A supplier with strong margins and idle capacity can absorb part of a six-point change to keep volume, and a supplier running at capacity has no reason to. The same nine-point change therefore produces different price outcomes for two buyers in the same category. The practical answer is to ask what the January change does to their 2027 unit price in writing, and to treat a vague answer as information in itself.

article_title: China Is Removing the Export Rebate That Funded Cheap Quotes
text: Why is China removing a subsidy that helps its own exporters?
answer: The Ministry of Finance's stated rationale is to curb involuntary competition — firms competing on price to the point of destroying their own margins — and to push industry toward higher-quality, greener production. That is a deliberate choice to make these exports more expensive, and it is stated publicly rather than disguised. For buyers, the strategic reading matters more than the arithmetic: the cheap pricing in these categories was partly policy-funded, and the policy is being withdrawn on purpose. Planning on the assumption that it returns is planning against the stated direction.

text: Twenty element symbols, five notices, fifteen active and five suspended — and a suspension that runs into November 2026. The legal position is published. The willingness to supply is not, and that is the number buyers cannot look up.

article_title: China's Rare Earth Controls Are a Licence Regime, Not a Ban — and November 2026 Is the Next Decision
text: Have the rare earth export controls been lifted?
answer: No. Some escalation measures were suspended; the earlier licence requirements remain in force. The October 2025 package, including the controls on overseas transactions involving Chinese-origin content and on rare earth technology, was suspended by Announcement No. 70 of 2025 for a defined period. What remains active is the baseline: Announcement No. 18 of 2025 covering seven medium and heavy rare earths, Announcement No. 10 of 2025 covering five strategic metals, and the earlier gallium, germanium and antimony controls. A suspension is a pause on a clock, not a repeal, and the suspended package remains the clearest available map of where the controls go next.

article_title: China's Rare Earth Controls Are a Licence Regime, Not a Ban — and November 2026 Is the Next Decision
text: Why is a licensing regime harder to plan around than a ban?
answer: A ban has a date, a scope and a negotiable status, so it can be modelled as an event. A licence regime has none of those properties. It adds documents, delay and legal risk to every individual shipment while leaving the material technically available, so the market does not reprice cleanly and buyers cannot tell a shortage from a supplier's decision to decline. The result is a supply chain where the legal position is published and the commercial position is not, and where identical products move freely for one buyer and stall for another in the same month.

article_title: China's Rare Earth Controls Are a Licence Regime, Not a Ban — and November 2026 Is the Next Decision
text: What does the November 2026 window actually decide?
answer: It is when the suspension of the October 2025 package reaches the end of its defined period. Three outcomes are possible: the suspension expires and the package returns, the suspension extends, or the package returns in revised form. The practical significance is that the suspended notices are the most ambitious part of the regime, reaching foreign-made products with Chinese-origin content and rare earth technology rather than only material leaving a Chinese port. Buyers with any Chinese-origin content in their bill of materials have exposure to that outcome.

article_title: China's Rare Earth Controls Are a Licence Regime, Not a Ban — and November 2026 Is the Next Decision
text: How much does a licence delay actually cost?
answer: The funding cost is smaller than most buyers expect, which is why it gets ignored. On a $120,000 shipment held ninety days at a 9% annual cost of capital, the interest is $2,663.01. Add port storage at $45 a day and it reaches $6,713.01. The number that matters is not on that table: it is the downstream commitment the shipment was feeding. A paused container in a critical-minerals chain stops earning but does not stop costing, and the missed delivery is the part that does not come back at the next negotiation.

text: Marketplaces went from 53% to 91% on Portal registration in one year, while listings reached 58% on the three data fields that decide whether a listing survives contact with an authority.

article_title: The EU's 2026 Compliance Sweep: 560 Orders, and the 58% That Should Worry Sellers
text: What exactly was checked in the 2026 sweep?
answer: National market surveillance authorities examined almost 1,700 online listings across 35 marketplaces between May and July 2026, focusing on children's articles and gym equipment. The checks looked specifically at whether listings identified an economic operator established in the European Union along with contact details, as the General Product Safety Regulation requires. The Commission published the results on 8 September 2026. Where listings failed, authorities issued enforcement orders to the marketplaces — 560 of them in total. The exercise was the second coordinated sweep since the regulation became applicable on 13 December 2024.

article_title: The EU's 2026 Compliance Sweep: 560 Orders, and the 58% That Should Worry Sellers
text: The marketplaces scored well. Why does that increase my risk?
answer: Because it makes enforcement cheaper. When 91% of marketplaces are registered on the Safety Gate Portal and every one of them has named a consumer contact point, an authority can identify the operator behind a listing and act through a working channel. In the previous year, with registration at 53%, the same authority faced a slower and less reliable route. The regulator's cost per action has fallen, and enforcement activity follows the cost of enforcement. The platform's improved score is a seller's reduced friction for getting caught, not a reduced risk of non-compliance.

article_title: The EU's 2026 Compliance Sweep: 560 Orders, and the 58% That Should Worry Sellers
text: Is a takedown a fine?
answer: No, and that distinction is why sellers under-prepare. A fine is a defined amount that appears in a budget line. A takedown is an interruption whose cost grows with duration and is set by an authority's timetable rather than the seller's. In the worked example, a single SKU selling 40 units a day at $29.99 loses $4,198.60 of contribution margin in 14 days and $13,495.50 in 45 days. The revenue returns only after remediation. Sellers who model the remediation effort but not the duration are modelling the smaller half of the cost.

article_title: The EU's 2026 Compliance Sweep: 560 Orders, and the 58% That Should Worry Sellers
text: Does this apply to sellers outside the EU?
answer: Yes, and it is the specific case the responsible person requirement addresses. A seller established outside the Union who sells into the EU market has to have an economic operator established in the Union named on the listing, with contact details, answering for compliance. A marketplace does not stand in for that person. Sellers who assume the platform's own regulatory registration covers their listings are reading the marketplace's obligation as their own. The 58% figure suggests that assumption is widespread, and the 560 orders suggest it is being tested.

text: One in 120: the break-even risk at which a $150 check beats an $18,000 deposit. Below that threshold, verifying a Chinese supplier's registration is not best practice — it is the cheaper side of a straightforward comparison.

article_title: China Put a Face Check on Company Registration — and Named the Agents Who File It
text: What changed on 1 May 2026 for Chinese company registration?
answer: The 2026 editions of the registration document and materials standards took effect, replacing the 2022 editions. The substantive addition is a real-name registration confirmation form, which records that the applicant confirmed their identity and the consistency of the registration matter, and which the registration authority must review. Personal identifiers, addresses and mobile numbers are moved onto a separate page for protection. The stated purpose is preventing fraudulent and impersonated registration. For a buyer, the practical effect is that the registered particulars of a company filing under the new standards are backed by a verification step rather than self-declaration alone.

article_title: China Put a Face Check on Company Registration — and Named the Agents Who File It
text: How do I use the agent registry in a supplier check?
answer: Ask the supplier which agent or agency filed their registration, then treat the answer as a test rather than a formality. The rule effective September 2025 requires agents to identify themselves in a national system and requires them to identify their clients and the beneficial owners of corporate clients, while retaining records for at least ten years. An agent operating inside that regime has documentary duties and a filing ban to lose. A supplier who cannot name who filed their registration is telling you something about how the registration was assembled, and that answer is worth more than the paperwork itself.

article_title: China Put a Face Check on Company Registration — and Named the Agents Who File It
text: Does the three-year ban apply to the supplier or to the agent?
answer: To the person designated directly responsible for the false registration, which can be either. The provision refuses filings submitted by a designated person acting as liaison or agent for three years from the date the registration is revoked. Note what it does not do: it does not automatically void the underlying registration, and it does not compensate a buyer who paid a deposit against it. The ban is a deterrent on the filing side of the market, which is precisely why the agent question is worth asking — the penalty lands on the party who assembled the file, not on the party who bought from it.

article_title: China Put a Face Check on Company Registration — and Named the Agents Who File It
text: Are the customs and payment rule changes part of the same check?
answer: They belong in the same review cycle rather than the same rule. The customs change added two conditional-mandatory items to the export declaration form, announced on 15 April 2026, with filing instructions in the single-window system; the text carries no effective date, so confirm the live date rather than assuming the announcement date. The foreign exchange consultation opened on 30 September 2026 and closes to comment on 30 October 2026; it is a draft with a blank commencement date. Neither replaces the registration check, and both affect how a supplier's paperwork behaves at the border and at the bank.

text: What actually changed on 18 June 2026?
answer: The compiling and publishing body for seven container indices transferred from the Shanghai Shipping Exchange to the Shanghai Shipping Research Institute (in Preparation), effective 18:00 that day. The seven are CCFI, SCFI, SCFIS, SEAFI, CICFI, TWFI and GCSP. Other shipping indices remained with the Shanghai Shipping Exchange. The same institutional change renamed the former exchange and merged it with the former Shanghai Municipal Transport Development Research Centre, and the container liner freight-rate filing function designated by the Ministry of Transport was retained. No index methodology change was announced alongside the transfer.

article_title: Your Freight Surcharge Points at an Index That Changed Owner in June
text: My contract names the Shanghai Shipping Exchange. Is it void?
answer: The publication is continuous and the index names are unchanged, so the practical position is closer to a stale reference than a void clause. The problem is verification: if the clause says the adjustment is calculated by reference to data published by a named entity, and that entity no longer publishes it, the buyer loses the straightforward ability to audit the number. The remedy is administrative rather than dramatic — a side letter or an amendment that names the index and the current publisher, agreed before the next adjustment cycle rather than during a dispute about one.

article_title: Your Freight Surcharge Points at an Index That Changed Owner in June
text: Why does the lane matter when the composite exists?
answer: Because they measure different baskets and they diverged. In the week ending 30 September, the CCFI composite moved 0.33% while the Southeast Asia Service rose 9.10% and the Europe Service fell 2.89%. A composite averages the lanes, so it moves least when the lanes move most in opposite directions — precisely the condition under which a composite-referenced clause produces an answer furthest from the shipper's actual experience. The composite is a useful market summary and a poor surcharge reference for a single trade.

article_title: Your Freight Surcharge Points at an Index That Changed Owner in June
text: Is the Suez extension relevant to the same calculation?
answer: Yes, as a separate input rather than part of the index. The Suez Canal Authority's Periodical No. 28 of 2026, dated 7 September 2026, extends Periodical No. 1 of 2026 with all its provisions for six months, from 1 August 2026 to 31 January 2027, for all vessel types. Canal terms affect routing and therefore the freight element on Asia-Europe trades, so they belong in the same cost review. What the authority did not publish in a machine-readable form is the toll percentage content of the underlying periodical, so the direction is confirmed and the magnitude is not.

article_title: The Polysilicon Tariff Never Says China — and Buying Cheaper Costs You More
text: Does Proclamation 11052 target China?
answer: The documents do not name China — neither the proclamation nor the companion rule contains the word. The reason Chinese-origin goods face the highest effective treatment is structural: the proclamation defines a list of Trade Agreement Partners whose Column 1 duty rate and Section 232 duty are capped at 15% combined, and China is not on that list. Chinese-origin goods therefore receive no combined cap and no drawback condition, so the full 15% applies alongside the minimum import price mechanism. Being precise about this matters for planning, because the exposure follows from the partner list rather than from anything specific to the product.

article_title: The Polysilicon Tariff Never Says China — and Buying Cheaper Costs You More
text: What is the difference between a minimum import price and a tariff?
answer: A tariff rate multiplies the value of the goods. A minimum import price sets a floor on the price at which goods enter and enforces it through the duty calculation. If your documentation shows a first arm's-length US sale at or above the floor, the specific tariff is zero and only the ad valorem duty applies. If your entered value sits below the floor and you file the documentation, the specific tariff equals the shortfall. If you file no documentation, the specific tariff equals the entire floor. The consequence is that a cheaper invoice produces a higher effective rate rather than a lower duty bill.

article_title: The Polysilicon Tariff Never Says China — and Buying Cheaper Costs You More
text: When do the duties take effect, and what happens before then?
answer: The minimum import price programme and the additional 15% duty apply to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on 4 December 2026. Before that date a separate stockpiling rule applies, effective from 22 September 2026 through 3 December 2026, which caps weekly import volumes for importers of record that registered with Customs on or after 6 August 2026, and prohibits further entries from existing importers bringing in volumes substantially above their historic averages. The pre-December window is therefore restricted rather than open.

article_title: The Polysilicon Tariff Never Says China — and Buying Cheaper Costs You More
text: Do the duties stack with everything else?
answer: Yes. The proclamation states that the duties imposed apply in addition to any other duties, taxes, fees, exactions and charges applicable to the products. Foreign trade zone treatment is also restricted: covered goods admitted to a zone on or after the effective date enter only under privileged foreign status, which removes the deferral that zone admission normally provides. Buyers modelling the change should add the two components to their existing duty stack rather than treat them as a replacement for anything.

text: €15 on €10. The charges on a three-item ten-euro parcel exceed the value of the goods, because the EU now charges per item rather than per parcel — and the same rules apply at every value level, including above the threshold that used to define the exemption.

article_title: The EU Now Charges by the Item, Not the Parcel — and Ten Euros Can Cost Fifteen
text: Has the €150 exemption been abolished or replaced?
answer: Replaced, and the distinction matters for planning. Council Regulation (EU) 2026/382 deleted the customs duty relief that applied to consignments whose intrinsic value did not exceed €150, and substituted a flat duty of €3 per item for consignments within that threshold. So the relief is gone and a charge stands in its place, with a stated sunset of 1 July 2028. Above €150 the €3 duty does not apply, because it only ever substituted for the relief. The separate Union handling fee does apply above €150.

article_title: The EU Now Charges by the Item, Not the Parcel — and Ten Euros Can Cost Fifteen
text: How is the charge calculated on a mixed basket?
answer: Per distinct item, at a flat rate, not on the value. A consignment containing a pen, a notebook and a key ring is three items, so it carries three times the per-item duty and three times the per-item fee regardless of what each item cost. Dutch Customs states the fee is charged per declaration line, which is the practical unit on the entry. This is why the charge as a share of value rises sharply as basket value falls, and why a cheap multi-item basket carries a higher effective rate than an expensive single item.

article_title: The EU Now Charges by the Item, Not the Parcel — and Ten Euros Can Cost Fifteen
text: Who actually pays the €3 and the €2?
answer: The declarant, in the first instance. The delegated regulation operationalising the €3 duty states that responsibility for paying it properly upon arrival lies first and foremost with the declarant — meaning the platforms and sellers, or the carrier or agent declaring the goods — and only residually with other persons including the consumer. The handling fee follows the same logic and is payable to the customs authorities at least once a month, at the moment the customs debt is paid. For a seller, that means the charge is a cost of the declaration route rather than a cost the consumer absorbs by default.

article_title: The EU Now Charges by the Item, Not the Parcel — and Ten Euros Can Cost Fifteen
text: Does anything come back if the customer returns the goods?
answer: The handling fee does not. Article 20(6) of Regulation (EU) 2026/2108 states that the Union handling fee is non-refundable, and the Irish Revenue Commissioners confirm in their guidance that the fee is not refunded even where the goods are faulty. The €3 customs duty is also non-refundable unless the goods are faulty. For any seller with a meaningful returns rate, that makes the charge a permanent cost on the returned population, and it belongs in the returns provision rather than in a working-capital forecast.

article_title: China's Factory-Gate Prices Turned Positive, and That Ends the Wait-for-Next-Year Trade
text: Does a rising PPI mean my supplier will raise prices?
answer: It means the cost base underneath the quotation is rising, and that a supplier with no offsetting efficiency is under pressure to pass it through. Whether the pass-through reaches your price depends on their capacity utilisation, the length of your contract and the competitive position in your category. The published figures describe the pressure, not the outcome. What the change of direction removes is the previous default, under which waiting reliably produced a better price. From here, the pass-through is a negotiation rather than a trend in your favour.

article_title: China's Factory-Gate Prices Turned Positive, and That Ends the Wait-for-Next-Year Trade
text: Should I budget on 3.8% or on 2%?
answer: They answer different questions. The August year-on-year reading of 3.8% describes the current quarter and the momentum in the series. The January-to-August average of 2.0% describes the year that has actually occurred. For a full-year sourcing budget the average is the defensible input, because it sums what happened rather than projecting the most recent month for twelve months. Use the current reading to decide how urgently to act, and the average to decide what to plan.

article_title: China's Factory-Gate Prices Turned Positive, and That Ends the Wait-for-Next-Year Trade
text: The driver is imported oil and metals. Is this actually a China story?
answer: Only partly, and the distinction is practical. The statistics bureau attributes the monthly move in significant part to higher international crude oil and nonferrous metal prices, with industrial upgrading supporting demand in some emerging sectors. That means the pressure originates outside China and passes through its manufacturing base. The consequence for a buyer is that the same input pressure appears in quotations from competing manufacturing countries, so origin switching does not solve it, while material or specification substitution addresses the actual driver.

article_title: China's Factory-Gate Prices Turned Positive, and That Ends the Wait-for-Next-Year Trade
text: What should change in how I negotiate?
answer: Two things. First, stop treating a flat renewal as the neutral outcome. On a positive drift rate, a supplier holding last year's price has conceded the drift, and that concession is worth naming. Second, negotiate the pass-through basis rather than the price: agree which published series the adjustment follows, how often it resets, and whether the supplier absorbs a share of it. That converts an annual argument about a percentage into a formula both sides can check, and it is far easier to agree while the index print is public than during a dispute about an invoice.

article_title: China Taxes the Metal on the Way Out, Then Zeroes It Once the Metal Has a Shape
text: Is an export duty different from a tariff on imports?
answer: It is the same kind of instrument applied at the other end of the transaction. An import duty is collected by the destination country when goods arrive; an export duty is collected by the country of origin when they leave. China's export duty is charged on the FOB value, so it lands inside the price a supplier quotes rather than appearing on your own customs entry, which is why a landed-cost model built only on import tariffs understates goods that carry one. Rates on the 2026 schedule run from a zero provisional rate to a 50 percent nominal rate on tin ore.

article_title: China Taxes the Metal on the Way Out, Then Zeroes It Once the Metal Has a Shape
text: Why does the same metal have different rates depending on its form?
answer: Because the schedule is an industrial policy instrument as well as a revenue one. Taxing the raw form and zeroing the processed form keeps the processing margin and the associated employment inside China while still permitting the finished material to be exported competitively. The pattern is legible across the metals in Annex 3: unwrought copper 30 percent nominal, copper scrap 30 with a 15 percent provisional, and every wrought copper line at zero provisional. Aluminium repeats it one level lower. A buyer choosing between forms of the same metal is choosing which side of that policy to sit on.

article_title: China Taxes the Metal on the Way Out, Then Zeroes It Once the Metal Has a Shape
text: What does the `ex` marker in the annex mean?
answer: The annex defines it in its own note: for a line marked ex , the provisional or export rate within that tariff line applies according to the specific product description rather than to the line as a whole. In practice it lets one grade of a metal be taxed differently from another grade sharing the same code — high-purity cathode copper appears both as a zero provisional rate and as a 5 percent rate under different descriptions in the same line. A buyer relying on a generic code without reading the description on the entry can therefore be charged a rate they did not expect.

article_title: China Taxes the Metal on the Way Out, Then Zeroes It Once the Metal Has a Shape
text: Does the plan also change what I pay on the way in?
answer: Yes, and favourably. The same plan grants provisional import duty rates below the most-favoured-nation rate on 935 goods, adds national subheadings for intelligent bionic robots, bio-aviation kerosene and forest ginseng to bring the total to 8,972 lines, continues conventional rates under 24 free trade agreements with 34 partner economies, and gives 43 least-developed countries zero tariff on 100 percent of their lines. It also cancels provisional rates and restores the MFN rate on micro motors, printing machines and sulphuric acid, so not every change runs one way.

article_title: The Postal Flat Fee Died in Four Days — Now the Route Itself Is Closing
text: Four days. The $200-per-item postal duty on Chinese parcels existed from 24 to 27 February 2026 and was then replaced twice more. The current position is not a rate at all — it is a question of which entry route remains open, and that closes further on 22 October 2026.

article_title: The Postal Flat Fee Died in Four Days — Now the Route Itself Is Closing
text: What does a China-origin postal parcel pay today?
answer: Ordinary tariff treatment: the Column 1 rate plus any Section 301 duty the goods carry, plus the merchandise processing fee, assessed on the value of each dutiable postal item. There is no flat rate and no per-item schedule in force. On a $300 apparel parcel at a 16% base rate and a 7.5% Section 301 rate, the duty and fees come to roughly $71.54, before the cost of preparing and bonding the entry, which is a per-shipment expense rather than a percentage.

article_title: The Postal Flat Fee Died in Four Days — Now the Route Itself Is Closing
text: Why did the $200-per-item figure disappear so quickly?
answer: Executive Order 14388 carried the per-item schedule into the new tariff note and, in the same paragraph, ended it for entries on or after 28 February 2026. The mechanism it substituted was a duty equal to the rate in Proclamation 11012, a Section 122 surcharge of 10% ad valorem with a 150-day statutory life. That surcharge expired on 24 July 2026 and was not extended. Two replacements in five months, and the coverage has not all caught up.

article_title: The Postal Flat Fee Died in Four Days — Now the Route Itself Is Closing
text: What changes on 22 October 2026?
answer: From that date CBP enforces the exclusion in 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(vi), which removes mail merchandise subject to Chapter 98 or Chapter 99 duties from postal informal entry. Since nearly all Chinese consumer goods carry a Chapter 99 Section 301 code, they lose that route. Entry type 13, the electronic informal entry under 91 FR 38007, waives the exclusion for participants and is currently the only informal channel open to them. Shipments subject to anti-dumping or countervailing duty, or to quota, are not eligible for it.

article_title: The Postal Flat Fee Died in Four Days — Now the Route Itself Is Closing
text: Is the exemption coming back?
answer: No. Pub. L. 119-21 repeals the de minimis exemption effective 1 July 2027. The suspension applies to all countries with no restoration date, and the statute removes the provision itself rather than pausing it. That distinction is the practical one for planning: a suspension can be lifted by an administrative act, while a repealed provision has to be re-enacted by Congress before it can return. The only surviving reliefs are the bona fide gift allowances of $100, and $200 for the Virgin Islands, Guam and American Samoa, together with informational materials and donations.

text: Why does the CBAM factor of 97.5 per cent not mean 2026 charges 2.5 per cent?
answer: Because it measures what is retained, not what is charged. The factor is the share of free allocation still in place, so 97.5 per cent of the benchmark is deducted before anything is charged, and 2.5 per cent of the benchmark is charged. For Chinese hot-rolled coil the deduction removes 1.33575 of the 3.5057 tonnes otherwise billed, which is 38 per cent of the bill.

text: Which regulation governs the default values, and what does a tonne cost?
answer: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1740, published 31 July 2026. Article 1(1) replaces Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2025/2621 in its entirety and Article 2 applies the replacement from 1 January 2026. The Commission's stated reason is transcription mistakes made when the 2025 tables were consolidated under time pressure. For most Chinese CN codes the values are unchanged, which is why a number from an older page looks right and cannot be verified. The per-tonne costs are in the table above; each is the corrected default value plus a 10 per cent mark-up, minus the benchmark multiplied by 0.975, times the quarter's price.

text: Four. China holds a named EU steel quota in four of the twenty-six categories, and not in the one that matters most. Category 1.A carries close to a third of the 18.35 million tonne total, and China's entire route into it duty-free is a residual pool of 5,564 tonnes a quarter shared with every other unlisted supplier in the world.

article_title: The EU Steel Quota Is Tightest Where China Has No Allocation at All
text: What is the EU steel out-of-quota duty in 2026?
answer: Fifty percent ad valorem, raised from 25 percent and applicable from 1 July 2026 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1384, recital 16. The rise is intended to reduce the risk of trade diversion, which the Commission judged the previous 25 percent rate under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/159 had failed to do. Recital 17 confirms the duty is additional to other duties that already apply to the same categories. So anti-dumping or countervailing duty on the same goods is not offset against it; the two are charged together, from the first tonne above quota. Below the quota the additional duty is zero, and the goods pay only the ordinary tariff.

article_title: The EU Steel Quota Is Tightest Where China Has No Allocation at All
text: Does China get a quota under the new EU steel safeguard?
answer: Yes, in four of the twenty-six categories, and every one is most-favoured-nation only. Read from Annex I of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1457: 182,996.85 tonnes in category 4.B under order 09.9838, 47,351.25 tonnes in 3.B under 09.9828, 142.36 tonnes in 1.B under 09.9816, and 19.91 tonnes in 3.A under 09.9826. In category 1.A, hot-rolled coil, China has no named allocation at all. The four add up to 230,510 tonnes a year, against 642,294.94 tonnes held by Turkey in category 1.A alone. The FTA half of each quota is closed to Chinese origin.

article_title: The EU Steel Quota Is Tightest Where China Has No Allocation at All
text: What can a Chinese exporter use instead of a named quota in category 1.A?
answer: Only the residual pool listed as "Other countries", order number 09.9600, which is 22,256.02 tonnes a year or 5,564.01 tonnes a quarter, shared with every other supplier that holds no named allocation in that category. It is administered first-come, first-served under Articles 49 to 54 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/2447, and it resets each quarter. For planning purposes it is not a channel a supplier can commit to.

article_title: The EU Steel Quota Is Tightest Where China Has No Allocation at All
text: Which charge is larger on Chinese steel, CBAM or the safeguard duty?
answer: On the published numbers, the safeguard duty. CBAM's cost on Chinese hot-rolled coil is EUR 163.53 a tonne at the Q1 2026 certificate price of EUR 75.36. The safeguard out-of-quota duty is 50 percent of CIF, which is EUR 250 a tonne at a CIF value of EUR 500 and EUR 350 at EUR 700. The duty is larger across the plausible range of steel prices, and it turns on a category number rather than on emissions.

article_title: Two EU Charges Hit the Same Tonne, and Only One of Them Is Knowable Up Front
text: Which charge is larger on Chinese steel entering the EU, CBAM or the safeguard duty?
answer: It depends on the product and the CIF value, and the answer flips between them. At a CIF value of EUR 500 a tonne, the safeguard duty is a flat EUR 250. CBAM ranges from EUR 144.13 a tonne for unwrought aluminium to EUR 539.91 for grain-oriented electrical steel. Flat steel and unwrought aluminium sit below the duty; every fabricated product sits above it. There is no single answer, which is why the per-tonne carbon figure should not be quoted as the cost of importing.

article_title: Two EU Charges Hit the Same Tonne, and Only One of Them Is Knowable Up Front
text: How do I work out where the two charges cross over for my product?
answer: Double the CBAM carbon cost for your CN code. That gives the CIF value per tonne at which the two charges are equal. For hot-rolled coil at EUR 163.53 a tonne, the crossover is EUR 327.08 a tonne. For screws and bolts at EUR 428.24, it is EUR 856.48. Below the crossover the safeguard duty is larger; above it the carbon cost is. The carbon figure is the only input you need, and it comes from your classification rather than your invoice — so if the crossover lands uncomfortably close to your actual CIF, the thing to check is whether you are on the right code at all.

article_title: Two EU Charges Hit the Same Tonne, and Only One of Them Is Knowable Up Front
text: Does the tariff-rate quota remove both charges or only one?
answer: Both, on the tonnage that enters inside the quota. A shipment admitted within the duty-free quota pays neither the safeguard duty nor, where the CBAM exemption does not apply, does the quota affect the carbon charge — the two are separate instruments and the quota only removes the safeguard duty. The practical point is that China holds named allocations in four of the twenty-six categories, so for most Chinese steel there is no in-quota route to use, and the residual pool available instead is 22,256.02 tonnes shared across every supplier without a named allocation.

article_title: Two EU Charges Hit the Same Tonne, and Only One of Them Is Knowable Up Front
text: Why is the carbon charge larger on fabricated steel than on flat steel?
answer: Because the CBAM default value scales with processing and the safeguard rate does not. The safeguard charges 50 per cent of CIF whatever the good is. The carbon mechanism charges for embedded emissions, and the published default values reflect how much more emissions-intensive fabrication is. Hot-rolled coil carries a default value of 3.187 tCO2eq per tonne; screws and bolts carry 6.375, roughly double. Fabricating a good roughly doubles its carbon charge while leaving the duty rate untouched, so the crossover moves up with every processing step.

text: Which is more expensive for a Chinese seller shipping low-value parcels, the US or the EU?
answer: It depends on the shape of the parcel, not on the market alone. On a EUR 300 consignment the US charge is roughly $91.54 to $131.54 against EUR 2.00 in the EU, so America is far more expensive. On a EUR 10 parcel of three items the EU charge is EUR 15.00, which is 150 per cent of the goods value, while the US charge is driven by an entry cost of $20 to $60 that exceeds the goods. Cheap multi-item parcels are worst off in Europe; fewer dearer parcels are worst off in America.

text: Why is the EU charge per item rather than a percentage?
answer: Because it is designed as a flat provisional duty while a permanent system is built, and a flat amount has to be attached to a unit. Council Regulation (EU) 2026/382 sets EUR 3 per item for consignments at or below EUR 150, and Regulation (EU) 2026/2108 adds a EUR 2 handling fee per item from 1 November 2026. The fee applies even above EUR 150, where the duty does not. That makes item count the single input that drives the EU charge, which is why consolidating a parcel into fewer items reduces it.

article_title: The Same Parcel Costs Three Times More in America Than in Europe
text: Does the US still have a per-item postal charge?
answer: No. The $80, $160 and $200 per-item postal charges were expected to become the new regime and ran for four days, from 24 to 27 February 2026, before being withdrawn. From 24 July 2026 a China-origin postal parcel pays its Column 1 duty plus any Section 301 list rate by classification, and the entry has to be filed. The per-item design still exists on the EU side; on the US side it was abandoned within a week of starting.

article_title: The Same Parcel Costs Three Times More in America Than in Europe
text: What should I check first before repricing for either market?
answer: Your own average order value and items per parcel, because they decide which regime binds. Then the classification question on the US side, since the base rate alone understates the charge once a Section 301 list rate applies, and Section 301 is why nearly all Chinese consumer goods lose access to postal informal entry under 19 CFR 145.12. On the EU side, confirm whether your consignments sit above or below EUR 150, because that decides whether the EUR 3 duty applies at all while the EUR 2 fee applies either way.

article_title: China Cut the Refund on Finished Goods and Added a Tax on Raw Metal
text: Is an export duty the same thing as removing an export tax rebate?
answer: No, and the difference is who the money moves between. A rebate is a refund of VAT the exporter already paid on inputs, so removing it withdraws a payment the state had made. An export duty is a new charge collected at the border on the way out. Both reduce what the exporter keeps per unit sold, and both end up in the FOB price, but one is the absence of a repayment and the other is a new tax. On the invoice the importer sees the same effect.

article_title: China Cut the Refund on Finished Goods and Added a Tax on Raw Metal
text: Which copper and aluminium products carry a Chinese export duty in 2026?
answer: The 2026 schedule lists 107 goods with an export duty, 68 of them at a provisional rate below the nominal one. Copper cathode is 30 per cent nominal, 10 per cent provisional; copper waste and scrap is 30 per cent nominal, 15 per cent provisional; ferrochrome is 40 per cent with no provisional relief. Unwrought aluminium is 30 per cent nominal, 10 per cent provisional. Every wrought copper and wrought aluminium line sits at a zero provisional rate, so the taxed forms are the raw ones.

article_title: China Cut the Refund on Finished Goods and Added a Tax on Raw Metal
text: How much does the rebate change add to a unit price?
answer: It depends on the FOB value and on how much of the loss the supplier passes through. The rebate on battery product lines was cut from 9 per cent to 6 per cent on 1 April 2026 and is cancelled on 1 January 2027, which is nine percentage points in total. On a $40 FOB unit at full passthrough that is $3.60 per unit and $3,600 per 1,000 units. The passthrough share is a negotiation, and the worked table shows the two stages separately because a supplier can absorb the first and pass on the second.

article_title: China Cut the Refund on Finished Goods and Added a Tax on Raw Metal
text: Why should I check the provisional rate rather than the nominal one?
answer: Because for most listed goods they differ, and for copper cathode the difference is a factor of three — 30 per cent nominal against 10 per cent provisional. Sixty-eight of the 107 goods carry a provisional rate. A buyer who reads only the headline schedule overstates the cost on cathode and on several other lines, and understates it where no provisional relief exists at all, as with ferrochrome at 40 per cent.

article_title: An Index-Linked Freight Clause Has Two Ways to Be Wrong, and They Are Independent
text: Why did the freight indices change publisher in 2026?
answer: Seven container indices transferred their compilation and release from the Shanghai Shipping Exchange to a new institute, effective 18:00 on 18 June 2026. The announcement is the exchange's own. For a contract the practical consequence is that the entity named in a surcharge clause is no longer the entity publishing the number, while the values continued under the new body — so a clause naming the old publisher needs checking rather than being treated as lapsed.

article_title: An Index-Linked Freight Clause Has Two Ways to Be Wrong, and They Are Independent
text: Does the CCFI composite represent the Southeast Asia lane?
answer: No, and the week ending 30 September 2026 shows how far apart they can be. The composite moved 0.33 per cent to 1923.93 while the Southeast Asia Service rose 9.1 per cent to 1322.15 and the Europe Service fell 2.9 per cent to 1970.38. A composite is a weighted mean of its routes, and a mean of moves in opposite directions sits near zero. The divergence that week was 8.77 percentage points, which on a $900 container is $78.97.

article_title: An Index-Linked Freight Clause Has Two Ways to Be Wrong, and They Are Independent
text: Does the SCFI include bunker and war risk surcharges?
answer: Yes, according to the Shanghai Shipping Exchange's published methodology. Individual SCFI route rates are described as the average all-in price covering spot ocean freight and related seaborne surcharges, and the list includes Bunker Adjustment Factor, Fuel Adjustment Factor, Low Sulphur Surcharge, Emergency Bunker Surcharge, Currency Adjustment Factor, Peak Season Surcharge, War Risk Surcharge, Port Congestion Surcharge and canal fees. Landside items such as terminal handling, security surcharges and inland on-carriage are excluded.

article_title: An Index-Linked Freight Clause Has Two Ways to Be Wrong, and They Are Independent
text: Does the CCFI include them as well?
answer: That is the question primary sources did not settle for me, and it is the one to settle before accepting or rejecting a surcharge demand on a CCFI-linked contract. The exchange publishes the two indices on different bases — SCFI covers Shanghai export spot rates across fifteen weighted routes, while CCFI covers national export container transport including contractual as well as spot rates — and the published SCFI definition does not establish the CCFI's. Get the definition in writing from the index publisher or the carrier rather than inferring it from the other index.

article_title: Two EU Charges Reach Steel and Only One Reaches Aluminium, and That Reverses the Ranking
text: Does CBAM apply to both steel and aluminium?
answer: Yes. CBAM covers iron, steel and aluminium among its sectors, so both metals carry a carbon charge on import into the EU. What differs is the amount, which follows the default emissions value for the CN code and the country of origin rather than anything about the material in the abstract. Chinese unwrought aluminium carries a default of 13.106 tonnes of CO2e per tonne of goods, while hot-rolled coil carries 3.187, and that fourfold gap is what produces the per-tonne difference. In our model the cost runs from EUR 100.11 on the cheapest Chinese steel line to EUR 981.88 on unwrought aluminium, both at the Q1 2026 certificate price of EUR 75.36 per tonne of CO2e.

article_title: Two EU Charges Reach Steel and Only One Reaches Aluminium, and That Reverses the Ranking
text: Does the steel safeguard apply to aluminium?
answer: The safeguard covers steel product categories: Regulation (EU) 2026/1384 and the allocation regulation that follows it set tariff-rate quotas across 26 product categories, and aluminium goods are not among the categories as published. That is our reading of the instruments and it is the basis of the comparison here, but we have not read the definition of each of the 26 categories line by line, so if your product sits near the boundary, check the category definitions in the allocation regulation's annex rather than relying on this.

article_title: Two EU Charges Reach Steel and Only One Reaches Aluminium, and That Reverses the Ranking
text: Which charge is larger on Chinese steel?
answer: It depends on the CIF value, because one charge is ad valorem and the other is not. The quota duty is 50 per cent of customs value; CBAM on hot-rolled coil is EUR 163.53 a tonne at the Q1 2026 certificate price. They are equal at a CIF of EUR 327.06 a tonne, so below that the carbon charge is larger and above it the quota duty is. Real shipments sit above it: at CIF EUR 700 the quota duty is EUR 350 against EUR 163.53.

article_title: Two EU Charges Reach Steel and Only One Reaches Aluminium, and That Reverses the Ranking
text: How much did doubling the quota duty add?
answer: At a CIF of EUR 700 a tonne, moving the out-of-quota duty from 25 to 50 per cent added EUR 175 a tonne. That increase on its own is larger than the entire CBAM charge on the same hot-rolled coil, which is EUR 163.53 at the Q1 2026 certificate price. At a CIF of EUR 500 the increase is EUR 125, which is smaller than the carbon charge, so whether the doubling exceeds CBAM depends on the goods value in the same way the total charge does. The rate was raised by Regulation (EU) 2026/1384, whose recital 16 gives the reason as reducing the risk of trade diversion, and recital 17 confirms the duty sits on top of other duties already applying to the same categories.

article_title: Two EU Charges Reach Steel and Only One Reaches Aluminium, and That Reverses the Ranking
text: Why does the aluminium figure not change with the goods value?
answer: Because CBAM is charged on emissions, not on price. The chargeable emissions for a CN code are a fixed number of tonnes of CO2e per tonne of goods, multiplied by the certificate price for the quarter of importation. So the charge is a fixed amount per tonne regardless of what the goods cost, which makes it proportionally more punishing the cheaper the goods are — the opposite of an ad valorem duty. At a CIF of EUR 700 the EUR 981.88 on unwrought aluminium is 140 per cent of the goods value; on goods worth EUR 2,000 the same charge is 49 per cent. The steel quota duty behaves in the reverse way, since 50 per cent is 50 per cent whatever the goods are worth.

article_title: CBAM Is Moving From Goods That Are Steel to Goods That Contain It
text: Is CBAM extending to downstream products?
answer: Yes, and the process is under way rather than finished. The Council of the EU reached a general approach on extending CBAM to downstream steel and aluminium goods on 12 June 2026, which is the Council's negotiating position rather than adopted law. The European Parliament's position follows, and the extension would apply from 1 January 2028. Because it is still in trilogue, the lists and the mechanism can both still change, so anything here should be read as the direction of travel rather than as a settled list of codes.

article_title: CBAM Is Moving From Goods That Are Steel to Goods That Contain It
text: What is an ex-code and why does it change who is covered?
answer: An ex-code is a tariff entry that captures only part of a good rather than the whole of it. In the proposed CBAM extension it captures only the steel or aluminium content of a downstream product, so the embedded emissions of a covered good are calculated from the metal inside it. That changes who is covered in a way a CN code list cannot express: under the current Annex I, a good either is on the list or is not, and an importer can tell from the customs declaration. Under an ex-code the question becomes how much metal the good contains and where that metal came from, which is a question about the product's bill of materials rather than about its classification. That is why the reporting duty, and not the charge, is the harder half of the extension.

article_title: CBAM Is Moving From Goods That Are Steel to Goods That Contain It
text: How much would the charge be on a typical appliance?
answer: It depends on the metal content and barely on anything else, since the charge follows the metal rather than the good's value. At the Q1 2026 certificate price of EUR 75.36 per tonne of CO2e, a tonne of steel carries EUR 163.53 and a tonne of aluminium EUR 981.88. So a washing machine containing 40 kg of steel carries EUR 6.54, which is 1.64 per cent of a EUR 400 appliance, and a refrigerator containing 50 kg carries EUR 8.18, also 1.64 per cent of EUR 500. The percentage stays low because appliances contain little metal relative to what they cost. A 40 kg steel content figure is illustrative; the real number is a fact about your product that your supplier has to confirm.

article_title: CBAM Is Moving From Goods That Are Steel to Goods That Contain It
text: Does the extension mean steel imports get cheaper or lighter?
answer: No, and the direction is the opposite of what a downstream extension suggests. Goods that arrive as steel are already inside the current Annex I, so a tonne of hot-rolled coil at CIF EUR 700 pays EUR 163.53, which is 23.4 per cent of its value. The extension brings in goods whose metal content is a smaller share of their value, so the new entrants face a proportionally lighter charge than the existing ones. Nothing in the extension reduces the burden on material imports; it widens the population rather than redistributing the cost.

article_title: CBAM Is Moving From Goods That Are Steel to Goods That Contain It
text: Why is material composition the hard part?
answer: Because it is a fact that customs data does not contain, and that most product documentation does not either. An import declaration states a classification, a value and an origin for the good as a whole. The extension requires the mass of steel and of aluminium separately, and the origin of each, because the embedded emissions are calculated from the metal. For a simple steel article that is nearly the same thing. For a machine with a steel frame, aluminium castings, and bought-in components of unknown provenance, it is a new dataset, built per SKU and per supplier, and it has to be in place before the first 2028 declaration rather than on it.

article_title: Your Supplier's Input Costs Rose 5.8%. Your 2027 Invoice Should Not.
text: Is the purchasing price index the price I pay?
answer: No. It measures what Chinese industrial enterprises paid for the raw materials, fuel and power they bought, including imported inputs. Your invoice is the price they charge for finished goods, which the producer price index tracks from the other side. The two are published in the same release and they are not the same number. What the gap between them tells you is the pressure the supplier is under, which is the starting position of a negotiation rather than its outcome. Treat 5.8% as the cost the factory is carrying, not as a price you owe.

article_title: Your Supplier's Input Costs Rose 5.8%. Your 2027 Invoice Should Not.
text: Which number should I put in a 2027 budget?
answer: Use the year-to-date averages rather than the August readings, because they describe a period that happened rather than a month that just ended. For the input side that is 3.2% and for the factory gate 2.0%. Then replace the composite with your own category rate, since the averages sit on top of a spread running from 19.8% for nonferrous metals and cables to -3.2% for building materials. A budget built on the composite is a budget built on an average of things you do not buy.

article_title: Your Supplier's Input Costs Rose 5.8%. Your 2027 Invoice Should Not.
text: Does a 5.8% input rise mean my quote goes up 5.8%?
answer: Not necessarily, and the output side is the reason. Producer prices for consumer goods fell 0.5% year on year in August, so a supplier in those categories is selling into a market where prices are not rising. Whether the input move reaches your invoice depends on the supplier's capacity position, the length of your agreement and the competition in your category. The published figures describe the pressure; the pass-through is a commercial outcome. What the data does establish is that the increase was not free for the supplier.

article_title: China's Factory Profits Rose 15.7%, and Their Customers Started Paying Later
text: What do China's industrial profit figures actually measure?
answer: They cover industrial enterprises above a designated size — the National Bureau of Statistics threshold, which excludes the smallest workshops — and report total profit, revenue, cost and a set of operating-efficiency indicators for the calendar period. The cumulative figure compares the year to a cumulative base, so it averages over the period and hides the recent rate; the release also gives the latest single month, which for August 2026 was 4.2 per cent against 15.7 per cent for the eight months. Both are in the same document and they answer different questions.

article_title: China's Factory Profits Rose 15.7%, and Their Customers Started Paying Later
text: Why does the receivables collection period matter more than the profit headline?
answer: Because it is cash, and cash is what a supplier uses to fund the next order. The release puts the average collection period at 72.2 days at the end of August 2026, up 0.9 days year on year, and finished-goods inventory turnover at 21.3 days, up 0.6 days. Profit margin improved to 5.66 per cent over the same period. So the earned money went up while the collected money slowed down, and the second one is what constrains a factory's ability to extend terms, absorb tooling or hold a price for a buyer.

article_title: China's Factory Profits Rose 15.7%, and Their Customers Started Paying Later
text: Which industries are the strongest and weakest in the release?
answer: The spread is the widest part of the data. Computer, communications and other electronic equipment manufacturing grew by 1.1 times over, non-ferrous metal smelting and rolling grew 82.9 per cent, and coal mining grew 51.6 per cent. Ferrous metal smelting and rolling fell 62.4 per cent, non-metallic mineral products fell 46.7 per cent, and automobile manufacturing fell 16.0 per cent. A buyer sourcing from the first group faces a supplier with room to hold a price; a buyer sourcing from the second faces one with slack pricing and a greater need for deposits.

article_title: China's Factory Profits Rose 15.7%, and Their Customers Started Paying Later
text: How should I use this in a negotiation?
answer: Separate the two questions. On price, use the industry figure for your supplier's category, because that is what determines how much room they have. On terms, use the sector-wide receivables number, because a stretched collection cycle pushes suppliers toward deposits and shorter payment periods before it pushes them toward a price increase. If your supplier's category is one of the declining ones, expect the terms conversation to come first, and prepare for it rather than treating it as a surprise.

article_title: China's Factory Profits Rose 15.7%, and Their Customers Started Paying Later
text: Is this different from the producer price index?
answer: Yes, and the two are worth reading together. The producer price index measures what factories charge; the profit release measures what they keep and how long it takes to arrive. We covered the price side separately in the analysis of the August factory-gate price reading, where the year-on-year change turned positive at 3.8 per cent. Profit growth alongside a stretched collection period means suppliers are holding price while waiting longer to be paid, which is a different condition from the one the PPI alone describes.

text: Twenty-one days, measured to the declaration. Not to loading, not to sailing, not to arrival. Distance sits outside the clock; waiting sits inside it.

article_title: China's Food-Export Container Check Expires in 21 Days, and the Clock Starts Before Loading
text: What does the 21-day validity actually measure?
answer: The interval between a passed container entering the qualified database and the export declaration being filed. The official guidance states that boundary, which is why the answer is not the obvious one. Ocean transit, port rotation and days at sea consume none of the window, because the declaration is already filed by then. Stuffing, inland haulage, yard time and document preparation consume all of it. A container that passed and then waited three weeks for a booking has no valid result left.

article_title: China's Food-Export Container Check Expires in 21 Days, and the Clock Starts Before Loading
text: Who files the application?
answer: The carrier, the stuffing unit or an agent for either, through the outbound container suitability module of the China International Trade Single Window, to the customs office where the container is stored. The useful question is not who is legally able to sign, because six categories of party can. It is who is named as the stuffing unit on the export declaration, because that line decides whose team files.

article_title: China's Food-Export Container Check Expires in 21 Days, and the Clock Starts Before Loading
text: What happens if validation fails at declaration?
answer: The declaration is rejected. Customs matches the container number against the qualified database automatically, and where the match fails the entry is refused and the receipt states that the number is not in the database. Nothing is charged and no penalty applies to the rejection itself. The cost is operational: refiling, a booking at risk, and — if the result expired rather than never existed — an empty container before re-inspection.

The floor on the processing fee for a formal entry is 12.5 times the fee for an automated informal one, and it is a floor rather than a rate, so it does not fall with the shipment. That single ratio is why removing the $250 ceiling is worth more to a small importer than anything else in this rule.

article_title: Your Parcel Is Getting Cheaper to Clear — and Harder to File
text: Does this rule change what I pay in duty?
answer: No. Duty is set by the tariff classification and the trade measures that apply to it, and the proposal does not touch either. It changes the processing fee, which is a separate line, and it changes which procedure the shipment is permitted to use. The $31.81 in the worked example is a fee difference on a $1,200 shipment, not a duty difference. The distinction matters because the two lines behave differently: duty scales with value and with the rate, while the processing fee on a small formal entry is a floor that does not move with either. A seller comparing quotes should keep them apart rather than blending them into one landed-cost percentage.

article_title: Your Parcel Is Getting Cheaper to Clear — and Harder to File
text: What happens on 7 December 2026?
answer: The comment window closes. CBP can then finalise the rule, and comments received after that date are not part of the record and carry no weight in the decision. Nothing in the proposal applies to a shipment entered today, so the deadline is a deadline for influence rather than for compliance. An agency finalising a rule of this size reads the comments that supply data it lacks: the bond premium filers actually pay, and the volume of shipments in the $251 to $2,500 band that the ceiling pushes into formal entry. An importer knows both and CBP does not.

article_title: Your Parcel Is Getting Cheaper to Clear — and Harder to File
text: Should I file a comment?
answer: If you import Section 232 goods in the $251 to $2,500 band, the amendment to 19 CFR 143.21 is the provision worth supporting in writing, and a comment describing your shipment volumes and the fee you currently pay is the kind of evidence an agency uses. If your concern is the bond requirement, note that CBP's own analysis argues the premium is unaffected by the liquidated-damages floor, which is an invitation to supply the premium data the rule omits. Comments go to docket USCBP-2026-0298. A comment naming a figure the agency cannot otherwise obtain is worth more than one restating a position.

article_title: Your Parcel Is Getting Cheaper to Clear — and Harder to File
text: Are mail shipments treated the same as other shipments?
answer: Not quite. Mail moves to entry type 13, a new electronic informal entry, and it carries two data elements that type 11 does not: a tracking number and the shipper or sender. Carriers also face an additional data requirement. The International Mail Duty Worksheet stops being used for this purpose, so a process built around emailing a spreadsheet on a monthly cycle is replaced by an entry filed with CBP Forms 3461 and 7501. The practical consequence for a seller is that the two new fields have to exist in your systems, or in your carrier's, before the filing can be made at all.

article_title: Your Parcel Is Getting Cheaper to Clear — and Harder to File
text: What applies today, before any of this is final?
answer: Entry type 11 can be filed on paper or electronically, entry is due within fifteen days after landing under 19 CFR 141.5, and the $250 ceiling on Chapter 99 goods remains in place, which is why the $31.81 is not yet available. The de minimis exemption remains suspended for all countries and is repealed from 1 July 2027 by Pub. L. 119-21. The fiscal 2027 fee schedule, by contrast, is in force now: the minimum formal-entry processing fee of $34.58 and the automated informal fee of $2.77 have applied since 1 October 2026, so the fee gap in the table is a present fact rather than a proposal.

article_title: Indonesia's Tarpaulin Duty Is $0.75 a Kilo, Not $0.0007 — and One English Page Says Otherwise
text: Is this an anti-dumping duty?
answer: No. It is a safeguard measure, which is a different instrument with a different test and a different scope. A safeguard applies when a surge in imports causes or threatens serious injury to domestic producers, and it applies to all origins rather than to named countries. Anti-dumping requires a finding that a particular exporter sold below cost or below home-market price, and it names the companies it hits. The practical difference for a buyer is that a safeguard cannot be escaped by changing supplier, because it does not name one, while an anti-dumping duty can sometimes be reduced by sourcing from an exporter that was not investigated.

article_title: Indonesia's Tarpaulin Duty Is $0.75 a Kilo, Not $0.0007 — and One English Page Says Otherwise
text: Why does the unit matter, and where does the per-tonne version come from?
answer: Because the duty is specific rather than ad valorem. A specific duty is a fixed amount per kilogram, so the total depends on the weight of the goods and not on the invoice value. If the unit is misread by a factor of a thousand, the per-kilogram figure becomes seven ten-thousandths of a dollar, which is small enough that a reader treats the whole measure as negligible and stops planning for it. The per-tonne version comes from a compilation rather than from the notifying document: the Chinese trade-remedy network's case page states the duty per kilogram in one paragraph and per tonne in another, and it is that page which English-language summaries tend to copy. The authority is the WTO corrigendum of 6 October 2026, issued to correct the heading of Table 7, which reads Specific Duty (Rupiah/kg) .

article_title: Indonesia's Tarpaulin Duty Is $0.75 a Kilo, Not $0.0007 — and One English Page Says Otherwise
text: Which products are covered?
answer: Polyethylene tarpaulins, identified in the notification as tarpaulins made from polyethylene (PE), under Indonesian tariff lines ex3921.90.70 and ex3926.90.99. The ex prefix means the line is covered only in part, so a shipment classified under the same heading is not automatically in scope and the description of the goods decides at entry. The investigation period ran from 2021 to 2024 and the case opened on 18 September 2024, so the data behind the determination is historical rather than current market evidence. If your product is a woven polyethylene sheet used for covering, it belongs in the analysis; if it is a coated fabric for another use under the same heading, it does not.

article_title: Indonesia's Tarpaulin Duty Is $0.75 a Kilo, Not $0.0007 — and One English Page Says Otherwise
text: What is the duty on one tarpaulin?
answer: That depends entirely on the sheet, because the rate is per kilogram and sheets vary in weight. The duty is 13,400 rupiah per kilogram in stage one, which is $0.7494 at 17,881 rupiah to the dollar. A 4 by 6 metre sheet at 200 grams per square metre weighs 4.8 kilograms and carries $3.60. The same sheet at 150 grams carries $2.70, and a 3 by 4 metre sheet at 200 grams weighs 2.4 kilograms and carries $1.80. Weight is the input and the rate is fixed, so the first thing to establish for each SKU is the entered weight rather than the value.

article_title: Indonesia's Tarpaulin Duty Is $0.75 a Kilo, Not $0.0007 — and One English Page Says Otherwise
text: When do the stages change?
answer: The notification describes three periods and gives a duty for each, without dating them. Implementation is left to an Indonesian finance ministry decree, and that decree is the document that will set the intervals between stages and the date the measure begins. Until it is published, treat the three figures as a known sequence with unknown timing rather than as a calendar you can plan shipments against. The amounts themselves are settled: 13,400, then 12,391, then 11,458 rupiah per kilogram, a decline of about eight per cent at each step.
